opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think that's actually a fair point, and I've never said these things are useless. People keep paying twenty dollars a month, and that tells you something real. People aren't fools. They're getting value out of it. The question is *what kind* of value, and whether it's the kind the hype claims.

My view has always been that these models are tremendous at what I call approximate retrieval. They're giant n-gram models on steroids, if you like. They're fantastic idea generators. If you want a first draft of an email, a cover letter, some boilerplate code, or a quick brainstorm, they're wonderful. In many of those cases you, the human, are in the loop as the verifier. You read the draft and fix the parts that are off. You run the code and see whether it breaks. The value is real precisely because the human is doing the part the model can't guarantee: checking correctness.

So when people say, "Look, millions of users prefer it, therefore it must be reasoning," I think that's a non sequitur. Subscriptions measure usefulness to a person with a verifier in their head. They don't measure whether the system can, on its own, produce a guaranteed-correct plan or proof. Those are very different claims. A calculator that's right ninety percent of the time would be a disaster. A brainstorming partner that's useful ninety percent of the time is a delight. Most consumer use falls in the second category.

There's also a selection effect. People quickly learn which tasks to give it and which not to. Nobody keeps subscribing because it solved their combinatorial scheduling problem with correctness guarantees. They keep subscribing because it saves them time on things where "pretty good" is good enough, or where they can easily check the answer.

That's why I've argued for what we call LLM-Modulo frameworks. You use the LLM as a generator of candidates and pair it with external verifiers or critics, whether those are model-based solvers, simulators, or humans. Then you get the best of both. The market is telling us the generation part is genuinely valuable. It isn't telling us we can throw away the verification part. If anything, the fact that the most satisfied users are the ones who know how to check the output is evidence *for* that view, not against it.

So yes, take the subscriptions seriously as evidence of value. Just be careful about what that evidence is actually evidence of.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts usefulness with guaranteed correctness and says subscriptions measure value rather than reasoning, but it does not clearly state that assistive technologies require a different evaluation strategy from autonomous technologies.

r002.rationale: It treats subscriptions as evidence that users get value, while explaining that they do not establish autonomous reasoning or correctness guarantees.

r003.rationale: It describes users checking, fixing, or rejecting model output, and says the value comes in part from the human verifying correctness.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful here, because people sometimes use continued subscriptions as a kind of trump card, right? "Look, millions of people are paying twenty dollars a month, so clearly these things are valuable, so stop complaining about reasoning." And I actually agree with the first part and disagree with the inference.

Let me separate the two things. I have never doubted that LLMs are useful. I use them. They are fantastic at what I would call the "idea generation" or "approximate retrieval" part of the work. If you want a first draft, a summary, a bunch of candidate names for a variable, a reformulation of something in a different style, they are genuinely wonderful, and people voting with their wallets is perfectly good evidence of that. That is the assistive setting, and in the assistive setting there is a human in the loop who is doing the verification. The human reads the draft, catches the thing that is off, fixes it, and moves on. So what the subscription is telling you is that the combination of the LLM plus a competent human is more productive than the human alone. That I completely believe.

What it does not tell you is that the LLM by itself is reasoning or planning in any robust sense. Those are different claims, and the market signal is almost silent on the second one, because the market is paying for the pair, not for the model in isolation. In fact, I would argue the reason the assistive mode works so well is precisely because the human is supplying the thing the model lacks, which is the ability to check correctness. That is the whole point of the LLM-Modulo framework we have been pushing: you let the LLM generate, and you have something, a human or a verifier or a solver, do the critiquing. The subscription numbers are, in a sense, confirmation that this generate-and-verify loop is valuable, and the human is the verifier in that loop.

Now, where I get a little worried is when people take user preference and start treating it as a proxy for correctness. Preference is not accuracy. People prefer confident, fluent, well-formatted answers. The model has been trained, through RLHF and so on, to produce exactly that. So you can get a very high preference signal on outputs that are wrong in ways the user did not notice. There is actually some evidence that users become less able to catch mistakes the more polished the output looks. So if your metric for "value" is "did the user keep paying," you might be optimizing for persuasiveness rather than for being right, and those can come apart in exactly the high-stakes cases where you care the most.

So my interpretation is something like this: continued subscriptions are strong evidence that these systems are valuable as cognitive tools in human hands, the way a calculator or a search engine or a very well-read but occasionally confabulating colleague is valuable. They are weak evidence, almost no evidence, about autonomous reliability. And the danger is that the commercial success of the first gets used as a rhetorical bridge to make claims about the second. I would like us to celebrate the first honestly, without pretending it settles the second. Those are questions you answer with careful, controlled evaluations where you actually know the ground truth, not with retention curves.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts subscription and preference signals for assistive use with controlled, ground-truth evaluations for autonomous reliability, indicating that the two require different evaluation approaches.

r002.rationale: It treats continued subscriptions as evidence that the human-plus-model combination is valuable, while saying retention does not establish correctness or autonomous reliability and that these require careful evaluations.

r003.rationale: It describes a human reviewing the model’s draft, catching errors, and deciding what to fix, showing that users can benefit while retaining discretion to reject answers.

astra-6.text:
I would take continued subscriptions as evidence that people perceive value in the system. If somebody keeps paying for an assistant, we shouldn’t dismiss that. But we have to be careful about what conclusion we draw. It doesn’t establish that the model is reliable, that its answers are correct, or even that it improves the user’s performance on every task.

User preference is an important signal, but it’s a different signal from correctness. You might prefer an answer because it’s fluent, reassuring, or agrees with your assumptions. So I would want to ask: Does this assistant actually help you accomplish what you intended? What happens when it makes a mistake? Can you recognize and correct that mistake?

An assistive system can be valuable without being independently competent at the entire task. The relevant unit of evaluation is often the human working with the system. Continued subscriptions tell us something about that relationship, but we still need to measure the outcomes.

r001.rationale: The response says evaluation should focus on the human working with the system, but it does not state that assistive technologies require different evaluation strategies from autonomous technologies.

r002.rationale: It treats continued payment as evidence that users perceive value, while saying this does not establish reliability or correctness and that outcomes still need to be measured.

r003.rationale: The response says an assistive system can be valuable without being independently competent, but does not clearly state that users retain discretion to reject its answers.

sol-6.1.text:
I would take continued subscriptions as evidence that people find some value in the system. If they keep paying for it, that tells you something. But it doesn’t tell you exactly what they value, and it certainly doesn’t establish that the system is reliable or that it improves their performance.

With an assistive system, the relevant question is what happens to the human–AI team. Does the person get better results? Do they catch mistakes? How much effort do they spend checking the output? A user might prefer an answer because it is fluent, reassuring, or agrees with them. That preference is real, but it is different from evidence that the advice is correct.

So I wouldn’t dismiss subscriptions or user preferences. They are useful signals of perceived utility. I would just be careful about turning them into a claim of demonstrated benefit. For that, you need to look at outcomes on the tasks people are actually trying to accomplish.

r001.rationale: The response discusses evaluating human–AI team outcomes, but does not state that assistive technologies require different evaluation strategies from autonomous technologies.

r002.rationale: It treats continued payment as a signal of perceived utility while saying that this does not establish reliability or demonstrated benefit.

r003.rationale: The response mentions catching mistakes and checking outputs, but does not state that users can reject the system’s answers.
